title: Hands-on teaching of complex tools: the example of GPMelt interactive tutorial
Building intuition for statistical reasoning:  Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) and p-values miscalibration
text:
Challenges


Modern biological experiments increasingly rely on high-throughput technologies that generate large datasets and create opportunities to test hundreds or thousands of hypotheses simultaneously. While this offers considerable scientific potential, it also introduces new statistical challenges that require additional caution during data analysis.
Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) control, and p-value calibration are therefore central concepts in modern biological research, yet many researchers struggle to develop an intuitive understanding of what they mean in practice. Although encountered routinely, the reasoning behind them is often perceived as abstract, mathematically complex, or inaccessible.
The communication challenge was compounded by the highly heterogeneous statistical backgrounds of the workshop’s participants, ranging from researchers with minimal formal training in statistics to others with substantial quantitative experience.
Another challenge was therefore not simply to explain statistical procedures, but to help participants build intuition and confidence, understand what changes when moving from single to multiple hypothesis testing, and develop the reasoning needed to engage with these concepts independently after the session.

title: Building intuition for statistical reasoning:  Multiple testing, False Discovery Rate (FDR) and p-values miscalibration

title: Striking image for GPMelt
text:
Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2024 Cécile Le Sueur)




This image captures the transformative power of GPMelt to fully explore the complexity of melting curve behavior.
The mosaic of non-sigmoidal curves in the background symbolizes the diverse range of melting profiles that GPMelt can integrate. Unlike state-of-the-art methods, GPMelt is agnostic to curve shape, breaking free from the constraints of sigmoidal melting behavior. Every curve — no matter how irregular — finds a place in the analysis, allowing for a more inclusive understanding of the thermal proteome.
Illuminated by the X-ray viewer, two non-sigmoidal curves emerge from the shadows. No longer obscured or discarded, they become fully accessible and visible, ready for interpretation. GPMelt brings these previously overlooked curves into the spotlight, making them a valuable part of the TPP-TR dataset. This comprehensive vision transforms our capacity to analyze protein thermal stability, opening up new possibilities for discovery.
The stethoscope, lit by the X-ray viewer’s glow, serves as a metaphor for GPMelt’s diagnostic power. It symbolizes the newfound ability of users to uncover and diagnose these unconventional curves. GPMelt doesn’t just detect atypical melting behaviors; it empowers users to explore the underlying biology, leading them toward novel discoveries. By fitting all curve types, including the most complex, GPMelt opens the door to advanced analyses like clustering, which could inspire hypotheses about the origins of non-sigmoidality and reveal deeper biological insights.
In essence, GPMelt is not just a tool; it’s a breakthrough that exposes previously hidden part of the meltome, pushing the boundaries of thermal proteome profiling and giving access to biological phenomena that were previously out of reach.

title: Visual thinking for scientific communication:  Designing visuals for clarity and engagement
text:
Challenges


The common challenge across these visuals is to translate complex concepts into intuitive visual representations without sacrificing scientific accuracy. Many of the ideas involved are abstract, interdisciplinary, or highly technical, making them difficult to communicate effectively through text alone.
Regardless of their communicative purpose, each visual therefore requires balancing multiple objectives simultaneously: accessibility for non-specialists, sufficient depth for expert audiences, clarity to support understanding and engagement, and enough visual appeal to attract and maintain attention.
The challenge is not simply to illustrate information, but to identify the visual representation that best supports understanding, highlights the key message, and communicates effectively across different backgrounds and communication contexts.





Approach


I design visuals as communication tools rather than decorative illustrations. The objective is not simply to represent information, but to support understanding through visual reasoning and synthesis.
Key principles:

simplifying complex ideas without losing their essential meaning;
combining abstract concepts with concrete visual representations to support intuition and understanding;
synthesising information from multiple disciplines or sources into coherent visual narratives;
using visual hierarchy, colour, and layout to guide attention towards the most important information;
adapting the style and level of detail to the intended audience and communication objective.





Strengths



Bridging audiences with different backgrounds through visual communication;
Distilling complex ideas into their essential communicable elements;
Condensing large amounts of information into clear visual summaries;
Designing visuals that support curiosity, reasoning, understanding, and decision-making;
Adapting visual communication across different stages of the communication process.






Impacts


Some concepts are difficult to communicate effectively through text, formulas, or verbal explanations alone, yet become immediately more accessible once visualised. By transforming abstract ideas into intuitive visual representations, these illustrations supported conceptual abstraction, knowledge translation, and information synthesis across a wide range of communication contexts.
These visual representations also provided a common language between disciplines. By translating abstract concepts, workflows, and analytical reasoning into intuitive visual forms, they facilitated discussions between researchers with different areas of expertise and helped communicate key ideas more efficiently.
More broadly, this work reinforced the idea that effective visuals are not merely decorative elements. When carefully designed, they can reduce the intimidation often associated with theoretical or highly technical content, making complex ideas more approachable while preserving their depth and meaning.

title: Scientific storytelling: Designing a high-impact conference poster
text:
Challenges


At large international conferences, poster sessions are highly competitive environments in which hundreds of projects compete simultaneously for attention. Standing out from the crowd is therefore essential to attract an audience before they move on to the next poster, often leaving only a few minutes to pitch the project.
For GPMelt, this challenge was amplified by the nature of the project itself. Advanced statistical methodologies can appear intimidating to researchers unfamiliar with sophisticated modelling approaches, creating a barrier not only to understanding the work, but even to initially approaching the poster and engaging with the presenter.
The challenge was therefore to create a poster that attracted attention, lowered this initial barrier, and encouraged researchers from diverse backgrounds to engage confidently with both the project and the person presenting it.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text: Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2026 Cécile Le Sueur)

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
The problem
Three factors compound the remaining inefficiencies. ` * First, the journal’s market position: unlike an established scientific journal, authors here aren’t always willing to comply with editorial requests, and the editorial team has to accommodate them to avoid losing manuscripts to competitors, since the journal is still establishing itself. * Second, the technical check remains manually intensive — authors reorder or rename sections despite the template and guidelines, and required information isn’t always in a consistent location, forcing manual copy-paste work. * Third, manuscripts vary in idiosyncratic ways that resist rule-based handling and often require case-by-case judgment.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
Workflow diagnosis
The earlier interventions (template, guidelines, technical checklist) solved the structural gaps in the workflow, but exposed a different kind of bottleneck: judgment calls that don’t reduce to a fixed rule set. A standard automation script can enforce “section X must exist” — it can’t decide what to do when an author reorders sections in a plausible but non-standard way, rename it or when a genuine exception should be accommodated to avoid losing a manuscript. That gap — needing reasoning and flexibility rather than rule enforcement — is what pointed toward agentic AI rather than further rule-based automation.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
Options considered

Extend the rule-based technical check further: add more explicit rules for known variations. Rejected: manuscript variation is too open-ended; rules would multiply indefinitely without covering genuine edge cases.
Manual case-by-case handling by editors (status quo): works, but doesn’t scale as the journal grows and consumes senior editorial time on low-judgment tasks.
Agentic AI workflow: an LLM-based system capable of information extraction, section reordering, and adaptive reasoning across manuscript variation — the option pursued, because it can flexibly reason through exceptions rather than requiring every exception to be pre-specified.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
Intervention (proposed)
Designed a framework mapping candidate AI interventions across the workflow, using GenAI itself to help identify bottlenecks and shape solution options — evaluating each step by AI opportunity, rationale, risk, and where human oversight remains necessary:










Workflow step
AI opportunity
Why AI
Risk
Human role




Technical check
Extract required info regardless of manuscript structure; reorder/rename sections to match template
Needs text understanding and flexible reasoning across varied structures — a rules engine can’t anticipate every exception
May misinterpret ambiguous content; risk of false negatives on real errors
Editor reviews flagged discrepancies before the manuscript proceeds


Manuscript correction
Spelling, grammar, and typographic conventions (e.g. non-breaking spaces before French punctuation)
Combines deterministic rules (typography) with contextual language understanding (grammar, style) faster than manual proofreading
Over-correction risk — altering author voice or flagging valid domain-specific terms as errors
Editor validates suggested corrections, especially domain terminology


Bibliography consistency check
Flag citations missing a reference entry (or vice versa); catch non-Zotero submissions with formatting drift
Requires matching content across two parts of a document and recognising equivalent citations in varied formats — beyond what the reference manager alone enforces
May mismatch similar-but-different entries; misses edge cases in unusual citation styles
Editor reviews flagged mismatches before publication


Whole-issue coherence check
Flag inconsistent notation/terminology across all articles in an issue; catch mistakes remaining after per-article correction
Requires holding and comparing content across multiple full-length documents at once — impractical to track manually with full recall
Risk of false positives on legitimate topic-driven variation; too many minor flags could overwhelm editors
Editor decides which flagged inconsistencies warrant issue-wide standardisation

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
Enablement & adoption
The rollout is planned in partnership with the production and IT teams, with the longer-term ambition of extending the approach beyond this journal to others across the company. The initial scope is deliberately narrow: a pilot on the current journal, with my own editorial team as first users. Training will cover practical use of the tool, but also serves a second purpose — building shared understanding of responsible AI use within the team. A feedback loop with the team is built into the design from the start, since the agentic workflow is expected to need correction as it encounters edge cases not yet anticipated.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
Impact (envisioned)
Reducing editorial time spent on repetitive, low-judgment tasks, freeing specialised editors’ time for higher-value work, and improving manuscript-handling consistency and turnaround — without imposing rigidity that risks losing manuscripts to competitor journals in a market where authors have alternatives.

title: From remaining workflow gaps to agentic AI intervention
text:
What I learned so far
Not every workflow bottleneck needs the same fix. Study Case 3 shows that templates and checklists solve structural gaps, where the requirement is clear and just needs enforcing.
This case is different: the gap isn’t a missing rule but a missing capacity to interpret meaning across variation — recognising that information is present but relocated, or that a section is mislabeled rather than absent.
Matching an interpretation-heavy problem to a tool built for interpretation, rather than defaulting to more rules or defaulting to AI everywhere, is the judgment this case actually demonstrates.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text: Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2026 Cécile Le Sueur)

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
The problem
Every article followed its own internal logic and style, with mandatory information frequently missing (author titles & affiliations, image copyright, sections, etc.). Correcting each article involved slow and tedious manual work. With only one editor on the team, the workload was becoming unsustainable.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
Workflow diagnosis
The root causes were structural, not individual effort: no article template existed, author guidelines were vague and incomplete, no reference manager was in use, and there was no formal technical check before a manuscript entered review. None of these gaps required advanced technology to fix — they required someone to notice they were gaps at all.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
Options considered

Reference management: a paid tool (EndNote, Mendeley) vs. Zotero — free, Word-compatible, no budget approval needed, and low enough friction that non-technical authors could adopt it directly.
Author guidelines: rewrite manually from scratch vs. use Gen AI to accelerate drafting a complete, clear version — chosen to move faster without compromising on the clarity the team needed.
Technical check: ad hoc, editor-by-editor judgment vs. a defined, explicit rule set every manuscript must pass before review — chosen for consistency and to make the check trainable and delegable, not dependent on a single editor’s memory.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
Intervention

Created a standard article template.
Rewrote and completed the author guidelines with Gen AI assistance.
Defined an explicit technical checklist manuscripts had to satisfy before entering the review stage.
Introduced Zotero as the team’s reference manager, building a complete tutorial (Gen AI-assisted) and training colleagues directly, changing the workflow so bibliographies were handled correctly at the source rather than corrected after the fact.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
Enablement/adoption
Each intervention paired a tool with matching documentation and training: the template went out to authors directly with clear instructions; the technical check was documented and taught to the specialised editors responsible for applying it; Zotero adoption was driven by a tutorial plus hands-on training for colleagues.

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
Impact

Manuscript quality improved — fewer missing mandatory sections, cleaner bibliographies.
Standardisation cut the editorial time spent reordering and normalising articles.
Author-facing back-and-forth over missing information dropped, now handled by a specialised team rather than the core editor.
Bibliography-related workload fell sharply, and the reference-manager switch avoided roughly €125 per article in costs previously paid to an external team.
Authors reported a clearer process (via the template) and better-aligned expectations with editors (via the guidelines).

title: From workflow gaps to pragmatic process improvement
text:
What I learned
Small changes can produce outsized effects on workload, quality, and cost.
Before reaching for AI, it’s worth checking whether a simpler, well-established tool or concept — like a template — already solves the problem; these are often faster to implement and just as effective.
Knowing your users well enough to pitch training at the right level is what actually determines whether a tool gets adopted or ignored.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text: Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2026 Cécile Le Sueur)

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
The problem
Biologists running these experiments typically have limited statistical training and limited computing experience. A framework that worked for developers and data analysts wasn’t automatically usable by a broader audience encompassing the biologists themselves.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
Workflow diagnosis
The framework itself wasn’t the barrier — access to it was. Through conversations with potential users, I identified four concrete requirements a usable version would need to meet:

it had to be easy to use,
non-intimidating (built on tools users already trusted),
genuinely understandable (not just runnable),
and deployable in whatever environment the user actually had — a personal laptop or an institutional HPC cluster — without ongoing dependency maintenance.

This reframed the task from “package a new probabilistic ML framework” to “redesign how the model reaches its users.”

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
Options considered

Distribute as a script or notebook: fastest to release, but assumes a statistical and coding fluency most biologists don’t have.
Package as a standard Python library (pip-installable): lower barrier than raw code, but still requires environment setup and command-line comfort most users lacked.
Containerize with Docker only: portable and dependency-free, but without workflow orchestration, still exposes users to technical setup.
Nextflow + Docker + dedicated documentation website: the option pursued — pipeline orchestration, containerized portability, and a plain-language explanation layer combined, minimizing the technical background required to use the tool.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
Intervention
Encapsulated the full framework — from model optimisation through results analysis — into an open-source Nextflow workflow, packaged with Docker so it runs identically on a personal laptop or an institutional HPC cluster, independent of underlying library updates (GitLab repository).
Built a dedicated website (GPMelt website, see also the dedicated page on the Communication portfolio) explaining both the statistical theory behind the model and the practical steps to run it, so users could understand what the tool is doing, not just execute it as a black box.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
Enablement/adoption
Maintained the user website as the primary point of entry for new users. Presented the tool at international conferences — two talks and two posters (see also the dedicated page for one poster on the Communication portfolio), with one talk receiving an award — to build visibility and credibility with the target scientific community.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
Impact
The redesigned framework became usable by a broad user base: any experimentalist, not just those with a statistics, computer science or ML background. It runs consistently across computing environments (laptop to HPC) without user-side maintenance, and the award-winning conference reception independently validated the approach beyond my own assessment.

title: Turning a probabilistic ML framework into a user-friendly tool
text:
What I learned
Building advanced technology to solve a complex problem is only half the work. People won’t use a method they don’t understand or can’t install and run in practice — user training, documentation, and support are a core part of a technology developer’s job, not an afterthought.
This meant translating user needs into concrete technical requirements and coordinating delivery with technical teams to complete my own expertise — in this case, institutional IT services and developers from the AI Health Innovation Cluster team at Heidelberg.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text: Click on the image to zoom in! (© 2026 Cécile Le Sueur)

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
The problem
Two constraints dominated the workflow: the cost of reagents and samples, and the workload of running and measuring them via mass spectrometry. Existing methods in the field ([3], [4]) addressed this by cutting sample count and measurement time — but only by discarding the shape of the melting curve, data that recent research suggests carries real biological signal. The field’s standard fix for the cost problem was quietly trading away information that mattered.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
Workflow diagnosis
Discussions with the experimental team surfaced the real bottleneck: existing approaches optimised the analysis method while treating the experimental protocol as fixed. Nobody had questioned whether the protocol itself needed to stay fixed while only the analysis flexed. Reframing the protocol as adjustable — not just the analysis — was the key step toward a viable solution.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
Options considered

Do nothing: keep the existing protocol; accept the cost/workload ceiling.
Adopt an existing fast method ([3], [4]): cuts cost and time, but sacrifices melting-curve shape data.
Redesign protocol and statistical model together: the option pursued — changing how data is collected and how it’s processed, so less raw data still yields statistically valid, shape-preserving results.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
Intervention
Proposed and prototyped an adapted version of the existing protocol (TPP-TR), designed to halve reagent, sample, and instrument-time consumption while preserving full melting-curve shape measurement — something existing fast methods couldn’t do. This required redesigning both ends: how the experiment was run, and how the existing ML framework processed the resulting, structurally different data, including new preprocessing and adjustments to the underlying statistical model to preserve replicate-level rigor. We refer to chapter 7 of [5] for technical details.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
Validation & enablement
Validated the approach on a test dataset as proof of concept. Presented the work at an international conference to build visibility and external credibility (see the dedicated page on the Communication portfolio), and worked directly with lab colleagues to walk through the trade-offs and build buy-in for the change. The project reached proof-of-concept stage rather than full lab rollout, due to time constraints within the PhD — but the statistical validation and conference reception indicate it’s ready for a lab to take further.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
Impact
For the same reagents, samples, and instrument time, the redesigned protocol was projected to double data throughput without reducing the replicate count needed for statistical confidence.
Beyond the immediate efficiency gain, this would reduce workload on already-stretched experimental teams and lower the cost barrier for labs to use the method at all — widening access to a technique otherwise limited to well-funded groups.

title: From probabilistic ML framework developement to workflow redesign
text:
What I learned
The instinct to reach for “more data” is often the wrong lever. The gain came from questioning an assumption everyone treated as fixed, and from understanding the constraints of the people doing the experimental work, not just the statistical ones.
Technology adoption isn’t only about better answers to the scientific question — it’s about redesigning the process around the people who have to live with it.

title: Communicating potential, not just results:  Persuasive scientific storytelling in a 10-minute conference talk
text:
Challenges


The talk targeted a diverse audience ranging from experimental biologists to computational researchers, most of whom were not specialists in Thermal Proteome Profiling.
The challenge was not only to explain the core idea clearly and accurately, but also to do so within a ten-minute conference format. This left very little time to introduce the scientific problem, explain the proposed solution, and persuade the audience that the idea mattered.
The communication challenge was further complicated by the structure of the message itself. The talk began with a highly specialised methodological problem before gradually revealing a broader question hidden beneath it: how reducing experimental costs could contribute to making advanced scientific methodologies more accessible. The key challenge was therefore to guide the audience from a niche technical concept to its wider implications without losing either scientific rigour or narrative momentum.

title: Adapting complex concepts to different audiences: from Gaussian Process intuition to formalism
text:
Challenges


Hierarchical Gaussian Process regression is a highly abstract statistical framework that can be intimidating even for quantitatively trained scientists. Yet, using GPMelt effectively requires understanding several interconnected concepts spanning multiple levels of abstraction, from the intuition behind Gaussian Process regression and its application to Thermal Proteome Profiling data, to the way biological experimental designs are represented within a hierarchical statistical model.
The communication challenge was therefore twofold: lowering the barrier created by mathematical complexity while preserving the concepts necessary for meaningful use of the method. At the same time, the resources had to work for audiences ranging from experimental biologists with limited statistical training to bioinformaticians and statisticians with very different levels of familiarity with Gaussian Processes.
The key challenge was to communicate the same underlying ideas across multiple levels of abstraction and audiences without sacrificing clarity, rigor, or engagement.





Approach


Rather than introducing the framework through mathematical formalism, I designed a series of short, visual-first videos that introduced the key concepts progressively, from intuitive explanations aimed at a broad audience to more advanced material for statistically trained users. The goal was not only to make the principles easier to understand, but to provide multiple entry points into the same underlying concepts.
Key design choices included:

prioritising conceptual understanding before introducing formal definitions;
adapting vocabulary, examples, and level of detail to each audience;
using visual metaphors, colour coding, and animation to make abstract concepts more tangible;
progressively increasing the level of abstraction, from intuitive explanations to more formal statistical reasoning.





Strengths



Adapting explanations to audiences with different levels of expertise;
Making complex concepts accessible without oversimplification;
Communicating across multiple levels of abstraction while preserving rigor;
Translation between disciplines and domains (e.g. from biological data to mathematical modelling; from statistical analysis to biological interpretation);
Connecting experimental, statistical, and computational perspectives;
Designing learning pathways that support progressive understanding, from intuition to formalization;
Creating high-quality visual explanations of abstract concepts (figures, animation, storytelling);
Developing concise, engaging educational content for self-directed learning.






Impact


These resources were designed to help users understand the reasoning behind the model, not only to learn how to use GPMelt in practice. By making the underlying statistical framework more approachable across different levels of expertise, they aimed to reduce the gap between method developers and end users.
This allows users to engage with the modelling framework at a depth appropriate to their needs and expertise, while maintaining a coherent conceptual link between the biological experiment and its statistical analysis. As a result, researchers can engage more confidently with the methodology, better understand its assumptions and limitations, and use the resulting analyses more critically and effectively.
Ultimately, the objective was to transform the model from a black box into a tool that users could meaningfully understand and build upon. By focusing on the underlying modelling principles rather than software usage alone, these resources provide a foundation for adapting and extending the framework to new experimental settings and data types.
